item.title: Theory of Anomalous Diffusion and Superdiffusion in Integrable Spin Chains
item.description: arXiv:2611.33274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrable systems can exhibit diffusive or Kardar--Parisi--Zhang (KPZ) scaling in two-point correlations even when their current full counting statistics (FCS) differ from those usually associated with these universality classes. We explain this separation using a multispecies particle gas that preserves the scattering structure of integrable spin chains. For anisotropy $\Delta>1$, large particles are advected by a mobile bath. The resulting FCS has a Gaussian-mixture form and approaches the M-Wright distribution at late times, with finite-time rounding due to mobile species. At the isotropic point $\Delta=1$, all particles are mobile, and the charge transfer by large particles is discrete. A self-consistent Poisson distribution describes the FCS, with a nearly Gaussian bulk and model-dependent, non-Gaussian tails. By contrast, two-point correlations follow from the statistics of a large tracer particle. For $\Delta>1$, it undergoes Brownian motion, yielding Gaussian spreading. At $\Delta=1$, we provide evidence from fluctuating hydrodynamics for the emergence of the KPZ Pr\"ahofer--Spohn scaling function in dynamical correlations and trace it to the finite coupling of the largest particles to a continuum of slower ones, with long-ranged velocity fluctuations. Our framework shows how universal dynamical two-point correlations coexist with distinct model-dependent current statistics.
item.dc:creator: Jitendra Kethepalli, Andrew Urilyon, Jacopo De Nardis

item.title: Extrinsic thermodynamic geometry, symmetry, and the cost of constraint
item.description: arXiv:2611.33443v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Driving a stochastic system in finite time costs excess work; exactly how much depends on which system parameters, and hence which paths in distribution space, a controller can access. In the friction-tensor formalism for slow driving, the space of equilibrium distributions is a Riemannian manifold and constraints on a controller define submanifolds. Whether a constrained controller is forced onto suboptimal paths is a question of the extrinsic thermodynamic geometry of the submanifold, which we develop for discrete systems. We show that submanifolds with zero extrinsic curvature can be identified from symmetries of the transition network, before any optimization. A minimum-work protocol on such a submanifold is therefore stationary in the excess work even when the constraints are lifted. The stationarity of symmetric optima holds exactly, beyond slow driving. In the slow-driving regime, we show that the ambient curvature transverse to a symmetric submanifold determines whether nearby symmetry-broken protocols have lower excess work. This curvature, which separates into independent contributions from each pattern of symmetry breaking, thus acquires an operational meaning as a measure of the thermodynamic incentive to break a given symmetry. A thermodynamic comparison theorem provides an inexpensive test of local minimality that weighs the extremal curvatures along the symmetric protocol against its excess work. There is no need for such tests under certain convexity conditions on the transition rates and control parameters, which guarantee that a symmetric optimum is a global optimum. These results certify the global optimality of a five-parameter protocol previously observed to match 15-parameter full control of a four-spin Ising system, and explain why partial symmetry breaking is optimal for the same system under local-field control.
item.dc:creator: Jordan R. Sawchuk, David A. Sivak

item.title: The Phases of Hierarchy
item.description: arXiv:2611.33566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a dynamical phase theory of hierarchy, in which depth decides whether a population of size $N$ that revises its own environment can correct it without overcorrecting. The statistics that let a large majority detect a small bias - the basis of the Condorcet jury theorem - also make its response grow as $\sqrt{N}$. Fed back into the environment it is judging, this sharpening destabilises the matched state through a flip bifurcation at a critical loop gain, which we obtain analytically for a class of models we term adaptive normal forms. We show that this instability can be attenuated by hierarchical layering, requiring a depth scaling logarithmically with $N$. This recovers known logarithmic bounds in organisational economics directly from dynamic stability conditions. Hierarchical depth carries its own costs however, and by analysing the signal chain transmission up the hierarchy we show that beyond a finite depth no correction reaches the top before its deadline, and that below it the cost of arrival grows exponentially with depth. A hierarchy that is too flat therefore oscillates and one that is too deep cannot be steered in time, leaving a bounded window of depth between an unstable flat phase and a frozen inertial phase. We further show that these results can be generalised by treating each layer as a real-space renormalisation step, classifying aggregation rules by how they transmit bias. This establishes a connection between these dynamic results to attention in Transformers, where a residual update is diffusion on the token graph and depth plays the role of scale. Finally we show these phase boundaries are observable in finite sampling, and propose measurements which may characterise the proposed phases in real adaptive systems.
item.dc:creator: Gerard McCaul

item.title: Universal Work Extraction from Individual Sequences by Finite--State Information Engines
item.description: arXiv:2611.33984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider information engines that interact with a heat bath at temperature $T$, a work reservoir, and a tape carrying an individual (deterministic) sequence $x$ over a finite alphabet $\X$. An engine is a cascade of autonomous ratchets with fixed energy levels and detailed--balance dynamics, each processing segments of $m$ tape cells and having finitely many internal states. We prove a converse bound on the extractable work in terms of the empirical block entropies of $x$,and show that it is achievable \emph{universally}, by engines whose energy levels do not depend on $x$. The maximal work per symbol is $kT[\ln|\X|-\bar H(x)]$, where $k$ is Boltzmann's constant and $\bar H(x)$ is the asymptotic normalized aligned block entropy of $x$, which equals its block Lempel--Ziv complexity, and the minimal work needed to erase $x$ is $kT\bar H(x)$ per symbol. Underlying these results is a two--way correspondence with universal coding: energy levels define a code, and a suitably operated cascade extracts $kT$ times $\ln|\X|$ per symbol minus the code length; conversely, a fluctuation identity shows that every engine fixed in advance defines a code. Hence, converses of universal coding apply verbatim to engines; e.g., the optimal redundancy of memoryless universal engines is given by the Shtarkov sum.
item.dc:creator: Neri Merhav

item.title: Exploring Physical Mechanisms Underlying the Emergence of Collective Order
item.description: arXiv:2611.33988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emergence of collective order from disordered constituents is a hallmark of active matter, and the Vicsek model (VM) serves as a paradigmatic system for its study. However, whether density-induced emergence in the VM differs between angular (intrinsic) and vectorial (extrinsic) noise, and what mechanisms govern the transitions, remain largely unexplored. Remarkably, we uncover that collective order emerges from a disordered state in a continuous-like manner under intrinsic noise but abruptly under extrinsic noise. Combining nonequilibrium landscape-flux theory with a coarse-grained mapping method, we show that the landscape evolves continuously from a single basin to two and back to one under intrinsic noise, but the two-basin landscape appears abruptly under extrinsic noise across the critical transition to flocking. The counterclockwise nonequilibrium flux sustains global circular motion, providing the driving force for reshaping the landscape. The mean flux and entropy production rate change steeply near the emergence threshold and exhibit pronounced peaks within the coexistence region, identifying them as the dynamical and thermodynamic origins of emergence. Our findings reveal a distinct abrupt emergence under extrinsic noise and offer deeper mechanistic insight, practical applications (e.g., locating phase boundaries and distinguishing transition types), and extensibility to other nonequilibrium collective systems.
item.dc:creator: Yitong Cai, Ruizhe Yan, Dongrun Jian, Jie Su, Jin Wang

item.title: Rotation curves of dwarf galaxies and dark matter as a condensate of $q$-deformed bosons: reconstruction and fits of the deformation profile
item.description: arXiv:2611.33999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dark-matter-dominated dwarf galaxies are a sensitive testing ground for models in which dark matter is a self-interacting Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC). In the Thomas-Fermi limit the standard BEC halo has the density profile $\rho\propto\sin(kr)/(kr)$, so that the shape of its rotation curve is fixed up to two scale parameters. Here we consider a condensate of $q$-deformed bosons. We show that, in the Thomas-Fermi limit, the deformation enters the structure of the halo only through the chemical potential of the condensate; consequently, a spatially uniform deformation parameter leaves the standard BEC profile unchanged. In every galaxy $\chi$ is depressed in the inner region, $kr\lesssim1$, relative to the outer halo, where it is approximately constant in most cases: the standard condensate describes the outer halo, while the core requires a weaker deformation, i.e., $q$ closer to unity. The profiles share this qualitative shape, but neither the depth nor the width of the depression is universal. Modelling the depression by a Gaussian, with two additional parameters, we fit the rotation curves with rms residuals of $0.6$--$2.6$~km\,s$^{-1}$, against $1.6$--$8.5$~km\,s$^{-1}$ for the standard condensate. According to the Bayesian information criterion, the deformed condensate is preferred over the standard condensate, the Navarro-Frenk-White profile, and the Burkert profile in four galaxies, is indistinguishable from the best of them in two, and is disfavoured in two. We discuss the limitations of these results, in particular the absence of error bars in the data, the neglect of baryons, and the phenomenological status of a position-dependent deformation.
item.dc:creator: Mahnaz Maleki, Asef Kheirandish, Morteza Nattagh Najafi, Hosein Mohammadzadeh

item.title: Energy plateau cascades from complex-time local quenches in thermal two-dimensional CFTs
item.description: arXiv:2611.33283v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work, we study local operator quenches in thermal two-dimensional conformal field theories with complex-time evolution, which can be viewed as an effective description of conditional dynamics in a system interacting with an environment. In contrast to quenches of the vacuum, the thermal initial state allows several conformal families to participate in the evolution. We show that their competition can produce cascades of approximately homogeneous energy plateaux, with successive plateaux approaching the energies of different primary states. Using conformal Ward identities on the cylinder and torus, we determine the local energy density and illustrate this behavior in free-field theories, the Ising model and Wess--Zumino--Witten models. We develop a cold-limit spectral description in which the dominant primary channel determines the height of each plateau, while conformal dimensions and operator matrix elements govern the transitions between them. For a fixed compact unitary CFT, we show that only finitely many primary channels can contribute to the leading plateau sequence. Finally, we discuss the large-central-charge regime, relating light-operator plateaux to few-particle sectors in thermal AdS and examining the limitations of this picture for heavy quenches.
item.dc:creator: Dmitry S. Ageev, Vladimir A. Bykov

item.title: Bosonic Magic Resources at Quantum Criticality
item.description: arXiv:2611.33306v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Non-Gaussianity is a resource for bosonic quantum information processing, providing a necessary ingredient for universal quantum computation in continuous-variable systems. Here we quantify non-Gaussianity in the ground state of the one-dimensional extended Bose-Hubbard model using quantum relative entropy (QRE), a measure determined solely by one-body correlations. The scaling of the QRE with system size reveals quantum phase transitions involving hidden and conventional order. We connect QRE scaling in the weakly interacting superfluid phase to Luttinger-liquid correlations and identify distinct critical signatures in its extensive and subleading contributions. At the Mott-Haldane transition, subtracting the extensive background reveals a pronounced peak in the subleading contribution, providing a clear signature of the onset of hidden string order. At the Haldane-density-wave transition, the extensive contribution to the QRE instead exhibits scaling consistent with Ising criticality. These results establish non-Gaussianity as a probe of many-body criticality, linking bosonic quantum resources to strongly correlated matter.
item.dc:creator: Paolo Stornati, Piotr Sierant, Emanuele Tirrito

item.title: Chiral Domain-Wall Modes in Topological Adaptive Quantum Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.33328v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum dynamical systems driven by both unitary evolution and measurements open a new landscape of nonequilibrium phases of matter. The role of topology in enriching this landscape remains less understood than that of entanglement and symmetry. A particularly interesting question concerns protected dynamical modes localized on spacetime domain walls between topologically distinct dynamical phases. These dynamical topological domain-wall modes (DTDMs) are well understood only for $0+1$D walls in $1+1$D fermionic dynamics. In this work, we study $1+1$D topological domain walls in $2+1$D charge-conserving free-fermion dynamics, modeled by topological adaptive circuits that steer the two sides of each wall toward a Chern insulator and a trivial insulator through measurements and feedforward corrections. Although the circuits target no particular wall state, each wall hosts $1+1$D chiral DTDMs. At long times in each quantum trajectory, they exhibit logarithmic scaling of entanglement and charge variance and algebraically decaying density correlations, surprisingly consistent with the ground state of a $1+1$D chiral free-fermion conformal field theory. This contrasts with purely $1+1$D charge-conserving free-fermion dynamics, which exhibits only area-law entanglement at finite measurement rates. We also show that the chiral DTDMs exhibit slow purification dynamics. When the system starts from a maximally mixed state, the DTDMs' entropy decays algebraically, accompanied by a vanishing Lyapunov gap, whereas each domain purifies on an $\mathcal{O}(1)$ timescale. Finally, we propose a physical picture for the long-time behavior of the DTDMs by treating the adaptive circuit model as a quantum cooling algorithm. Our results show that topological phases of adaptive dynamics can protect chiral modes on spacetime domain walls against repeated wavefunction collapse and Born-rule randomness.
item.dc:creator: Asadullah Bhuiyan, Haining Pan, Chao-Ming Jian

item.title: Identifying Renormalization Group Interfaces of Massless WZW Flows $\widehat{\mathfrak{su}}(2)_k \to \widehat{\mathfrak{su}}(2)_1$
item.description: arXiv:2611.33354v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A renormalization-group interface encodes how a flow relates operators at short and long distances. We identify this interface up to topological dressing for the conjectured massless $\widehat{\mathfrak{su}}(2)_k \to \widehat{\mathfrak{su}}(2)_1$ Wess-Zumino-Witten flows at every odd level $k\geq 3$. Global $SU(2)$ symmetry requires the interface to preserve a diagonal current algebra at level $k+1$, built from the currents on its two sides. The $\mathbb{Z}_2$ center symmetry then selects which representation labels the interface. This identification predicts distinct patterns of low-lying interface excitations for flows to the same infrared fixed point. Spin-chain calculations reproduce these patterns for $k=3$ and $5$, providing independent evidence for both conjectured flows.
item.dc:creator: Yuma Furuta, Yuya Kusuki, Toshiki Onagi, Yin Tang

item.title: Quantifying combined rate- and noise-induced transitions in a multiscale system
item.description: arXiv:2611.33449v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Excitations in multiscale dynamical systems produce persistent but impermanent excursions away from a quiescent state. A novel mechanism for inducing excitations, through a combination of rate-dependent parametric and stochastic forcing, is discussed using the FitzHugh-Nagumo model as an example. In the absence of noise, a quasithreshold separating the state space between supercritical and subcritical behaviour is defined with respect to slow manifolds associated with the metastable excited state. This is formulated in an autonomous system framework, which can be obtained via a compactification of time. Techniques from singular perturbation theory elucidate how canard trajectories shape the geometric structure of the quasithreshold as the system's pullback attractor moves through it. The probability with which weakly stochastically driven sample paths travel through the quasithreshold and undertake (i) solely noise-induced and (ii) combined rate- and noise-induced excitations is estimated numerically for each of the corresponding forcing scenarios, using the adaptive multilevel splitting algorithm. The probability of weak stochastic forcing preventing a rate-induced excitation, which occurs deterministically, is likewise estimated. This quantifies the different rates at which the probability of each transition scenario scales exponentially with the noise strength, in accordance with sample path large deviation principles. It is revealed that a combination of (deterministically subcritical) parametric and stochastic forcing is exponentially more likely to induce excitations than stochastic forcing alone, which is attributed to the pullback attractor and quasithreshold converging towards one another.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Deeley, Peter Ashwin, Ulrike Feudel

item.title: Optimal Controlled Quantum Instrument for Monitored Many-Body Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.33472v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Post-selecting rare trajectories of monitored quantum dynamics requires exponentially many repeated experiments. We extend Bayes' rule to monitored many-body dynamics and bias the quantum trajectories by nonlinear functions of the post-measurement state. For functions that are constant on the sets of a suitable finite partition of the post-measurement states, we construct a quantum instrument on the system and an additional register that produces the biased trajectories at the optimal rates without post-selection. This optimal controlled quantum instrument has a natural tensor-network representation as the left canonical form of the system--register tensors. We illustrate the construction with two examples: a precessing qubit, biased by its spin component along the field, and free fermions with gain and loss, biased by the particle number, where the biased trajectories undergo a phase transition. We also argue, under one assumption, that biasing a measured Majorana chain by its von Neumann entropy leads to entanglement transitions.
item.dc:creator: Jimin Li

item.title: Noise-induced Extinction in Hierarchical Food Webs
item.description: arXiv:2611.33569v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Every finite population is eventually driven to extinction by demographic noise, even when the deterministic dynamics have a stable coexistence state. We develop a large-deviation theory of this process for hierarchical food webs of arbitrary size. In a community of $N$ species, the basal species $X_1$ reproduces intrinsically and every consumer may prey on all species below it, so that omnivory is built into the interaction graph. For unit conversion efficiency and self-limitation confined to the basal species, the mean-field dynamics have at most $2^{N-1}+1$ feasible fixed points. We prove that the sign of each passive eigenvalue equals the sign of the extinct species' density in the enlarged community, that every partial community containing $X_1$ is a saddle with one unstable direction for each extinct consumer, and that the coexistence state is the only stable fixed point. A WKB treatment of the master equation gives a $2N$-dimensional Hamiltonian whose fluctuational fixed points are obtained in closed form. The resulting extinction network has $3^{N-1}$ fluctuation-driven transitions, and its coarse-grained dynamics yield an exact recursion for every mean extinction time. We analyse the three-species omnivory module in full, including a minimal set of existence conditions, global stability of coexistence, numerical instanton actions for all nine transitions and the most probable extinction route, which we confirm with stochastic simulations. Finally, we show how deleting a single trophic link reshapes the extinction network.
item.dc:creator: Varun Nevash, Eric Forgoston, M. Ani Hsieh

item.title: Exclusion and internal structure in the association/dissociation kinetics of DNA-binding proteins in the fast diffusion limit
item.description: arXiv:2611.33740v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In many canonical biophysical and biochemical contexts, complex diffusing DNA-binding proteins undergoing nonspecific adsorption and desorption can exist in different conformational states. Equilibrium binding theories and kinetic models of competing ligands provide a basis for describing these systems. Coupling the internal conformational kinetics of bound proteins to exclusion and diffusion requires tracking both protein positions and binding states. Closed-form, tractable mathematical models that accurately describe the stochastic dynamics of structured proteins that bind to and diffuse along DNA are lacking. Here, we develop a new coarse-grained stochastic model of nonspecific DNA-protein binding in the fast diffusion regime, from which we derive an effective Markov model and its corresponding mean-field approximation that incorporates protein footprint size and conformational switching. We fit our new model quantitatively to previously measured dynamics of Replication Protein A (RPA) binding to ssDNA. Finally, by including multisegment binding states, our analysis captures facilitated exchange, revealing how multisegment architecture balances high affinity with rapid remodeling. Our theoretical model applies broadly to many other DNA-binding protein systems, including nucleosomes, ssDNA-binding proteins, and other multisegment complexes, providing accurate predictions and new strategies for evaluating experimental data.
item.dc:creator: Xiangting Li, Tom Chou

item.title: Controlling truncation errors in loop tensor network renormalization
item.description: arXiv:2611.33807v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: At finite bond dimension $\chi$, tensor network renormalization (TNR) of a critical model eventually becomes gapped. For LoopTNR with $O(2)$ symmetry on the $c=1$ critical line of the six-vertex model, parametrized by the Luttinger parameter $K$, we show that the correlation length $\xi$ of the gapped phase is set by the seed of the dimerization injected by the truncation, and depends on $\chi$ only through it. Read from a weak-coupling window early in the same run, the seed predicts $\xi=10^3$-$10^{16}$ via the sine-Gordon mass-coupling relation with no free parameter, to within a few percent for $K\le1.5$ and about 10% at $K=1.75$; since the seed fluctuates strongly with $\chi$, $\xi$ is not monotonic in $\chi$. An alternation of the vertex weights shifts the seed; with its sign read from a $\pi$ twist, one short calibration predicts a counterterm that delays the breakdown in 16 of the 17 compensated groups of a campaign fixed in advance. A correction of the coarse-grained tensors, repeated during the flow, keeps the runs at $K=1$ and $1.5$ critical up to step 160, the last step computed, and exposes the marginal truncation error that remains. Our findings illustrate a systematic procedure for controlling the relevant truncation error, and thereby extending the critical window, in tensor network renormalization at finite bond dimension.
item.dc:creator: Rikuto Fushio, Kokin Cho, Yuta Yamamoto, Akira Otsuki, Masahito Yamazaki

item.title: Unified preparation of exact and asymptotic quantum many-body scars from Dicke states
item.description: arXiv:2611.33987v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a unified quantum algorithm for preparing exact and asymptotic quantum many-body scar (QMBS) states in the spin-1 {\it XY}, domain-wall-conserving, and Onsager scar models. Model-dependent isometries map the exact scar states to Dicke states and the target asymptotic QMBS states to gapless magnon excitations of the spin-1/2 ferromagnetic Heisenberg chain. Exact QMBS states are prepared by applying the inverse isometries to Dicke states. For asymptotic QMBS states, block encoding first prepares the magnon excitations from Dicke states to a prescribed fidelity, after which the inverse isometries map the prepared states back to the physical chains. At fixed target fidelity, the block-encoding success probability has a positive lower bound independent of system size and scar index, implying that a constant number of amplitude amplification rounds suffices. Our algorithm enables systematic studies of nonergodic dynamics on programmable quantum simulators.
item.dc:creator: Yuki Asari, Masaya Kunimi, Tetsuro Nikuni

item.title: Discrete truncated Wigner approximation of the quantum phase transition in the transverse-field Ising model
item.description: arXiv:2611.34004v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The discrete truncated Wigner approximation (DTWA) has been a workhorse for large-scale spin dynamics, but whether it captures dynamics across a quantum phase transition has not been tested systematically. In this work, we use the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) to study the quantum phase transition with DTWA from one to three dimensions and with all-to-all connectivity, using slow linear ramps and fast ramps. We find that DTWA cannot capture the dynamics on the one-dimensional chain, and that its behavior is consistent with classical thermalization, in which its classical spins relax toward a thermal state at a finite effective temperature that does not vanish for slow ramps, while a one-dimensional chain cannot order at any finite temperature. For square and cubic lattices, in contrast to the chain, DTWA builds order, and the order sets in close to the quantum critical point found by quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, its correlations do not grow with the Kibble-Zurek exponents, so DTWA captures the onset of order but not the universal dynamics of the transition. For all-to-all coupling, DTWA follows the exact growth of the order parameter along the entire ramp. Our results suggest that DTWA becomes more reliable as each spin interacts with more partners, and that beyond one dimension it can indicate where a quantum phase transition lies but cannot capture its critical scaling.
item.dc:creator: Tuan-Vu Truong, Hoang-Long Nguyen

item.title: Reconstructing massive quivers on a defect circle
item.description: arXiv:2611.34129v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the kink and particle spectra for the massive $\phi_{2,1}$-deformations of minimal models $\mathcal M_{k+1,k+2}$ via truncated conformal space approach (TCSA) on a defect circle. The massive $\phi_{2,1}$-deformation preserves a set of non-invertible symmetries, furnishing a fusion category $\mathcal C_k\simeq {\rm SO}(3)_k$. These non-invertible symmetries are spontaneously broken, and thus label the vacua and organize the kinks and particles into their multiplets in terms of quiver diagrams. We employ a finite-volume truncated Hamiltonian approach on defect Hilbert spaces, $\mathcal H_{X_i}$ for $X_i\in\mathcal C_k$, to study these quivers in the IR theories. The symmetry defect can then close an individual kink on a circle. We first establish the relation between states of definite fractional momentum on the defect circle and physical kink and particle states labelled by their vacuum pairs. Using form factors of local fields, we independently measure the squared amplitudes between the states of the two bases in defect TCSA. Combining these measurements with defect TCSA spectra, we reconstruct the quiver diagrams for $k=3,4,5$ without assuming them in advance. In particular, for $k=4$ we reconstruct the distinct quivers of the ordered and disordered phases. For $k=5$, we identify the quivers of both the light and heavy multiplets.
item.dc:creator: Ting-Kai Chen, Jin Chen

item.title: Tripartite entanglement dynamics following a quantum quench
item.description: arXiv:2408.12533v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the dynamics of multipartite entanglement after quenches from initial states which generate multiplets of quasiparticle excitations beyond the usual pair structure. We focus on the dynamics of tripartite entanglement through the lens of the Markov gap -- a computable quantity that signals irreducible tripartite entanglement when positive. In the tight-binding chain, we show that the Markov gap is positive at intermediate times, implying the presence of tripartite entanglement. After a time delay, the Markov gap increases and then decays at longer times, thus exhibiting an entanglement barrier. We argue that those qualitative features are consistent with an interpretation of the spreading of tripartite entanglement by triplets of tripartite-entangled quasiparticles.
item.dc:creator: Cl\'ement Berthiere

item.title: The flux of particles in a one-dimensional Fleming-Viot process
item.description: arXiv:2601.16029v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Fleming-Viot process describes a system of $N$ particles diffusing on a graph with an absorbing site. Whenever one of the particles is absorbed, it is replaced by a new particle at the position of one of the $N-1$ remaining particles. Here we consider the case where the particles lie on the semi-infinite line with a biased diffusion towards the origin which is the absorbing site. In the large $N$ limit, the evolution of the density becomes deterministic and has a number of characteristics similar to the Fisher-KPP equation: a one-parameter family of steady state solutions, dependence of the long time asymptotics on the initial conditions, Bramson logarithmic shift, etc. One noticeable difference, however, is that in the Fleming-Viot case, the solution can be computed explicitly for arbitrary initial conditions and at an arbitrary time. By modifying the diffusion rule near the origin, one can produce a transition in the flux of absorbed particles, very similar to the pushed-pulled transition in travelling waves. Lastly, when a cut-off of order $1/N$ is added to the hydrodynamic equation, we find corrections of order $(\ln N)^{-2}$ or $N^{-\gamma}$ to the flux of absorbed particles, depending on whether the front is pulled or pushed, as for the correction to the velocity in travelling waves.
item.dc:creator: \'Eric Brunet, Bernard Derrida

item.title: Breaking of clustering and macroscopic coherence under the lens of asymmetry measures
item.description: arXiv:2602.15969v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In one-dimensional systems, spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) states are fragile by nature, as the injection of a non-zero energy density above the ground state is expected to restore the symmetry. This instability implies that local perturbations can lead to macroscopic correlation profiles, a breaking of clustering properties and even macroscopic quantum superpositions. In this work, we investigate the effect of interaction on this phenomenology by considering an interacting model with conserved domain wall number, that possesses a ferromagnetic ground state breaking the Z2 symmetry of the Hamiltonian. We first show that a local quench in this system amplifies quantum interferences, producing a macroscopic magnetisation profile that directly reflects the scattering phase of the model. Then, we use two asymmetry measures, namely the Entanglement Asymmetry (EA) and Quantum Fisher Information (QFI), to characterise the quantum coherence associated with the fluctuations of the magnetisation. By focusing on subsystems comparable in size to the light-cone of the perturbation, we confirm the emergence of macroscopic quantum coherence throughout the whole perturbed region. Finally, we discuss the link between EA and QFI and show that the variance/EA inequality for pure state can be generalised to a QFI/EA inequality for mixed states.
item.dc:creator: Florent Ferro

item.title: Energetics of stochastic limit-cycle oscillators: when does coupling reduce dissipation?
item.description: arXiv:2604.24553v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Non-linear oscillators occur in a wide range of biological and engineered systems. In noisy environments, the steady-state entropy production rate (EPR) quantifies time irreversibility and, under a thermodynamic interpretation, the associated energy dissipation. We study an idealized, analytically tractable family of stochastic circular limit-cycle oscillators and examine how mutual coupling in pairs and populations alters dissipation. The dynamics are characterized by a dimensionless effective temperature given by the ratio of radial relaxation and diffusion timescales. For identical oscillators, we derive analytical results for the EPR under radial, phase (Kuramoto-like), and Cartesian couplings. The phase-coupling analysis also considers nonidentical intrinsic frequencies. Coupling can increase or decrease EPR through changes in the radial mean and variance and in probability currents, with the response depending on effective temperature and system size. In particular, weak attractive Cartesian coupling lowers the EPR of identical oscillators at any effective temperature. At sufficiently low effective temperature, full Cartesian coupling produces a finite-coupling minimum below the uncoupled EPR throughout the oscillator family considered. Reduced EPR can also accompany improved individual and collective temporal coherence.
item.dc:creator: Anton F. Burnet, Vansh Kharbanda, David Tobias, Benedikt Sabass

item.title: Geometric Formulation of Power-Efficiency Bounds in Carnot-like Engines
item.description: arXiv:2605.02732v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We formulate the power-efficiency constraint of Carnot-like heat engines as a geometric optimization problem in the plane of normalized branch dissipations. In this plane, efficiency contours are straight lines, so maximizing the efficiency at fixed power reduces to bounding the slope of an admissible line. For branch dissipations that scale inversely with a power of the process time, the fixed-power constraint defines a two-dimensional attainable region, and the resulting slope-bound problem reduces to a linear-programming problem. This geometric framework yields the exact power-efficiency constraint for Carnot-like heat engines with power-law dissipation.
item.dc:creator: R. X. Zhai

item.title: Norms, overlaps and Yangian descendants for the Haldane-Shastry spin chain
item.description: arXiv:2606.20168v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Haldane-Shastry spin chain is a prototypical integrable model with long-range interactions, notable for hosting quasiparticles with fractional statistics and serving as a discrete analogue of a conformal field theory. Its remarkable simplicity is closely tied to a full Yangian spin symmetry. While the highest-weight states for this symmetry are known explicitly, a systematic treatment of the descendant states, needed for the computation of various physical quantities, has remained incomplete. In this work, we provide a detailed construction of these descendants in terms of the algebraic Bethe ansatz following recent work of Ferrando et al. In the limit of extreme twist, it includes the Gelfand-Tsetlin basis. As an application, we derive product and determinant formulae for norms and overlaps of these states.
item.dc:creator: Yunfeng Jiang, Jules Lamers, Yuan Miao

item.title: Renormalization for Robust Memory without Synchronization
item.description: arXiv:2610.40651v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Local error correction can preserve classical information against noise, but protection under synchronized updates need not survive when sites evolve at independent random times. Establishing stability is particularly challenging when protection relies on the collective action of competing local rules. Here we develop a spacetime renormalization framework that reveals how independently acting local updates can collectively stabilize memory. We identify sufficient conditions under which the geometry of stable interfaces and suppression of defect propagation produce reliable erosion at large scales. Applying this framework, we prove the stability of the asynchronous R squeezing code and introduce robust processes in two and three dimensions. In these systems, both encoded phases persist under sufficiently weak noise, even when the noise favors one phase. Our results provide a criterion for designing autonomous memories sustained by competing local stochastic dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Shashwat Chakraborty, Jong Yeon Lee

item.title: Mutual Linearity in Nonlinear Population Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.14501v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mutual linearity, the persistence of affine relations among stationary observables under arbitrarily strong changes of one transition rate, is known for Markov jump processes and chemical reaction networks. We show that generalized Lotka--Volterra dynamics form a new class of mutually linear systems, even though species can go extinct and attractors can be chaotic. Any change to one species' equation acts on the others as one effective press and keeps all abundances affinely related: piecewise across extinctions, and as time averages on chaotic attractors.
item.dc:creator: Shiling Liang

item.title: From Growth Inhibition to Fluctuations: Testing an Ising Model of Bacterial Responses to Antibiotics
item.description: arXiv:2611.31609v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Complex networks of biochemical reactions have been proposed to exhibit emergent cooperativity that can be described by an effective Ising model, with a small number of parameters encoding collective interactions. Here this mapping is experimentally tested using the response of three bacterial species to a range of antibiotics acting on different cellular targets. The Ising description is compared to the conventional Hill model, examining both the mean growth-rate response and, importantly, its population growth-rate heterogeneity (PGRH). While both models describe the mean growth-rate dependence on antibiotic concentration comparably well, we find that the Ising model provides a markedly better description of PGRH, offering an additional and more stringent test of the collective description. The fitted Ising interaction strength is systematically related to the Hill exponent and increases with the functional distance of the antibiotic target from the protein-production machinery. These results provide experimental support for describing complex biochemical reaction networks through effective cooperative Ising interactions, and suggest that the collective response of bacterial growth to antibiotics reflects the organization of the underlying metabolic network.
item.dc:creator: Pietro Cicuta, Morten Kals, Nir S. Gov

item.title: Lattice models of chiral random motion: A short review
item.description: arXiv:2611.32743v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chirality, a systematic rotational bias, is ubiquitous in many random motion patterns, from bacteria cells, that swim in circles near surfaces and spinning colloids, to charged particles diffusing under the influence of magnetic fields. In two dimensions, chirality renders random transport \textit{odd}: the diffusion tensor acquires an antisymmetric part that leaves the mean-squared displacement invariant but modifies fluxes and boundary currents. Lattice models for random motion are a natural setting to study chirality, since they are exactly solvable, connect directly to heterogeneous media, cellular automata, and programmable robots, and in discrete time admit fully chiral limits with a localised bulk and edge transport. Lattice walks with a rotational bias have been introduced in different communities several times since 1960, yet without a common language or conceptual connection between them. Here we review these models from the perspective that on the lattice, chirality requires memory. Taking the recently introduced chiral random walk model as a template, we describe the walker with an internal degree of freedom. With a chiral biased updating rule, the full diffusion tensor of this chiral walker turns odd. Within this picture, we can unite persistent and chiral walks, run-and-tumble motion, and cyclic random motions in one framework. We discuss how the memory is followed into the environment; in Lorentz lattice gases, kinetic and rotor walks, and random odd environments; and into the path; in spiral self-avoiding walks.
item.dc:creator: E. Kalz, J. Wojcik, J. Uhlig, N. Sherf, Y. Roichman, R. Metzler

item.title: Tomographic Electron Flow in Confined Geometries: Beyond the Dual-Relaxation-Time Approximation
item.description: arXiv:2503.14461v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hydrodynamiclike electron flows are typically modeled using the Stokes-Ohm equation or a kinetic description that is based on a dual-relaxation-time approximation. Such models assume a short intrinsic mean free path $\ell_e$ due to momentum-conserving electronic scattering and a large extrinsic mean free path $\ell_\text{MR}$ due to momentum-relaxing impurity scattering. This assumption, however, is overly simplistic and falls short at low temperatures, where it is known from exact diagonalization studies of the electronic collision integrals that another large electronic mean free path $\ell_o$ emerges that describes long-lived odd electron modes---this is sometimes known as the tomographic effect. Here, using a matched asymptotic expansion of the underlying Fermi-liquid kinetic equation with multiple electron relaxation times, we derive a transport theory for tomographic flows in arbitrary smooth boundary geometries. Our key results are a set of governing equations for the electron density and electron current, their slip boundary conditions (which are applied at diffuse boundaries), and boundary layer corrections near diffuse edges. We find that the tomographic effect strongly modifies previous hydrodynamic theories for electron flows: In particular, (i) a local equilibrium is established in the bulk, where the flow is governed by Stokes-Ohm-like equations with significant finite-wavelength corrections, (ii) the velocity slip condition at the boundary is strongly modified and not accounted for by the widely used hydrodynamic slip-length condition, (iii) a large kinetic boundary layer of width $\sim\sqrt{\ell_e \ell_o}$ arises near diffuse boundaries, which is much larger than in conventional near-hydrodynamic theories, and (iv) all these effects are strongly suppressed by an external magnetic field. We illustrate our findings for electron flow in a channel.
item.dc:creator: Nitay Ben-Shachar, Johannes Hofmann

item.title: The role of entropy production and thermodynamic uncertainty relations in the asymmetric thermalization of open quantum systems
item.description: arXiv:2510.05072v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The asymmetry between heating and cooling in open quantum systems is a hallmark of nonequilibrium dynamics. Here, we investigate the thermalization of a quantum system weakly coupled to a bosonic thermal bath under detailed balance, focusing on the entropy production rate and the quantum thermokinetic uncertainty relation (TKUR). Within the sector of states that remain diagonal in the energy basis we derive a perturbative expression for the time-dependent entropy production rate by expanding the relative entropy around equilibrium in terms of Liouvillian eigenmodes. Through this expansion, we determine that the spectral gap, the overlap of the initial state with the slowest decay mode, and the mode weight control the entropy production. Particularly for the thermal qubit, the ratio of the initial rates of heating and cooling has an exact closed form. Heating involves a higher initial entropy production, and hence faster thermalization, solely because of its larger spectral gap, i.e., the bath-temperature dependence of the dissipative rate. The TKUR is then used as a diagnostic tool that relates the asymmetry to the precision bounds on heat-current fluctuations. The analysis presented here is intended to clarify the thermodynamic origin of the asymmetry within the well-controlled Markovian case.
item.dc:creator: \'Alvaro Tejero

item.title: Tunable many-body burst in isolated quantum systems
item.description: arXiv:2602.09665v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Thermalization in isolated quantum many-body systems can be nonmonotonic depending on an initial state. We demonstrate that a burst---a transient deviation from thermal equilibrium---can be created at a designated time from a low-entangled initial state for a nonintegrable mixed-field Ising chain, by developing a systematic numerical method to construct such a low-entangled state. Contrary to the typical spreading of information, the created burst is accompanied by a slow or even negative entanglement growth. We analytically show that a burst becomes probabilistically rare after a long time. Our results suggest that a nonequilibrium state is maintained for an appropriately chosen initial state until quantum scrambling becomes dominant. Our predictions can be tested by quench experiments with programmable quantum simulators.
item.dc:creator: Shozo Yamada, Akihiro Hokkyo, Masahito Ueda

item.title: The Quantum Kicked Rotor: A Paradigm of Quantum Chaos. Foundational aspects and new perspectives
item.description: arXiv:2604.12316v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The kicked rotor provides a simple yet powerful model for introducing many of the central concepts of classical and quantum chaos. Despite its apparent simplicity, it exhibits rich dynamical behavior and has found applications across a wide range of fields, including atomic and optical physics, condensed matter physics, and emerging quantum technologies. This chapter begins by exploring foundational ideas using the kicked rotor as a unifying framework. We first discuss the transition from regular to chaotic motion in the classical system, and then introduce key quantum phenomena such as dynamical localization and quantum resonances. Special attention is devoted to the emergence of characteristic time scales and their role in the quantum-classical correspondence. To make these ideas more concrete, we also provide a brief overview of experimental realizations of the kicked rotor and its variants, illustrating how theoretical concepts are implemented in practice. In the second part of the chapter, we guide the reader toward more recent and advanced developments. Topics include near-resonant dynamics, topological features of kicked systems, the emergence of quantum dynamical phases inferred from classical transport properties, and extensions to non-Hermitian physics. We conclude with a discussion of open problems and future perspectives, outlining directions in which the kicked rotor continues to offer valuable insights.
item.dc:creator: Giuliano Benenti, Giulio Casati, Jiangbin Gong, Zhixing Zou

item.title: Variational approach to droplet motion on uneven solid surfaces, including contact line dynamics and evaporation
item.description: arXiv:2605.12393v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show how dynamical equations for liquid films and drops on uneven surfaces, including contact line dynamics and evaporation/condensation effects, may be formulated as a variational dynamics, generated via Onsager's variational principle. The theory applies in the isothermal overdamped-dynamics limit. We apply this general approach to obtain several well-known results on contact line dynamics and to study drops pinning and sliding on inclined corrugated surfaces. This approach constructs the dynamical equations starting from the free energy of the system and therefore has the advantage that it naturally incorporates the correct equilibrium properties.
item.dc:creator: Gyula I T\'oth, David N Sibley, Agnes J Bok\'anyi-T\'oth, Dmitri Tseluiko, Andrew J Archer

item.title: Volatility Forecasts with Market Trends
item.description: arXiv:2606.20145v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show how volatility forecasts for financial markets can be refined by accounting for the current trends in these markets. Empirically, volatilities tend to increase day after day in times of strong up- or down-trends. This effect is particularly pronounced during down-trends. We find that it can accurately be modeled by including quadratic polynomials of the current trend strength as explanatory factors. Such factors can improve the predictive power of a wide range of volatility models, ranging from linear EWMA-based models over GARCH models and range-based models to stochastic volatility models. Our results are based on a robust statistical analysis of three decades of daily futures prices across equity-, bond-, FX- and commodity markets.
item.dc:creator: Sara A. Safari, Christoph Schmidhuber

item.title: Two-dimensional stealthy hyperuniform polycrystalline disk packings
item.description: arXiv:2606.23628v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Polycrystals consist of grains of local crystalline order separated by grain boundaries. Conventional polycrystals are generally not hyperuniform because their randomly sized and oriented grains sustain long-wavelength density fluctuations. We use collective-coordinate optimization to generate ultradense, two-dimensional polycrystalline packings of identical disks that are stealthy hyperuniform (SHU): their structure factor vanishes over a finite range of wave numbers around the origin. We compare them with nonhyperuniform polycrystalline disk packings generated by a modified Lubachevsky-Stillinger (LS) rapid compression algorithm, a molecular dynamics protocol that models conventional polycrystalline microstructures. We compare two-point statistics, grain-size distributions, specific surface area, diffusion spreadability, and the imaginary part of the effective dynamic dielectric constant. At high packing fractions, the grain-size distribution of SHU polycrystals exhibits a peak at a characteristic size, reflecting long-range correlations between grains. This peak is absent in LS polycrystals. SHU packings also exhibit enhanced long-time diffusion spreadability. Within the nonlocal strong-contrast expansion, dielectric SHU packings are perfectly transparent to electromagnetic waves at small wave numbers, whereas LS packings retain finite attenuation. Although SHU polycrystals are not generally expected to form spontaneously, long-range interactions or correlated substrates may provide routes to their formation. They can also be fabricated as metamaterials by nanolithography or 3D printing.
item.dc:creator: Carlo Vanoni, Paul J. Steinhardt, Salvatore Torquato

item.title: Dynamical Complexity of Projected Ensembles: A Geometric Quantum State Approach
item.description: arXiv:2608.09705v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the emergence of complexity in finite-size quantum systems as their dynamics transition from closed and coherent evolution to interacting and effectively open behavior. Using a state-based geometric framework, we represent mixed quantum states as probability measures on complex projective Hilbert space. Obtained by conditioning on the environment in a fixed basis, these geometric quantum states coincide with the projected ensembles that underlie deep thermalization and emergent quantum state designs. This representation allows us to track how interactions reshape the underlying pure-state geometry. We introduce two complementary diagnostics, a distinguishability measure based on the Wasserstein distance between nearby projected ensembles, which quantifies sensitivity to initial states, and a state-space coverage index, which measures long-time exploration of the subsystem state space. Applied to the quantum kicked top, both diagnostics generally increase with interaction strength. Their dependence on environment size is structured by parity symmetry, with integer-spin systems often exhibiting greater sensitivity and state-space coverage than half-integer-spin systems. These results highlight finite-size quantum effects and provide a geometric approach to quantifying dynamical complexity deep in the quantum regime.
item.dc:creator: Komal Sah, Fabio Anza, Alexandra M. Jurgens, James P. Crutchfield

item.title: Statistical Mechanics of Non-Abelian Learnability Transitions
item.description: arXiv:2608.19325v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Monitored many-body quantum systems can undergo sharp learnability transitions characterized by how much information can be learned by the observer. When the dynamics conserves a non-Abelian charge, such as an $SU(2)$ spin, understanding how the observer learns the total charge remains an outstanding problem. Unlike the Abelian case, where charge measurements on distinct sites commute, the $SU(2)$-symmetric readouts are noncommuting fusion measurements, making learning a genuinely quantum inference problem. We propose a theory of $1+1d$ monitored quantum dynamics with $SU(2)$ symmetry, and show that it can be described by an effective replicated loop model comprised of a replica-pairing field and a diffusive ($z=2$) background sector that carries the $SU(2)$ charge and remains gapless throughout the phase diagram. Our theory predicts that the "spin-sharpening" and entanglement transitions coincide as a single transition, which is supported by numerics. Ordering of the pairing field produces volume-law entanglement and hides the background sector from measurements, leading to a learning time of $t\sim L^{3}$ for the total spin. When the pairing field disorders, the background sector alone gives logarithmic entanglement and a diffusive learning time $t\sim L^{2}$. Our analysis is controlled by a large-loop-fugacity expansion.
item.dc:creator: Ruochen Ma, Romain Vasseur

item.title: Systematic and accurate anharmonic formation free energies of metastable defects via a constrained Bayesian Adaptive Biasing Force framework
item.description: arXiv:2608.20902v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Computing the formation free energies of metastable defects at finite temperature remains challenging due to anharmonicity, the multiplicity of basins and the frequent occurrence of migration events. Using the previously introduced constrained Bayesian Adaptive Biasing Force method (BABFc) [1], we establish a practical framework for computing restricted anharmonic formation free energies associated with individual metastable defect basins. We demonstrate that BABFc can be exploited as a robust, systematic and numerically efficient tool for addressing a long standing bottleneck in atomistic materials science: the finite temperature thermodynamic characterization of metastable defects in complex, highly anharmonic energy landscapes. The proposed workflow requires only a reference local minimum and a confinement strategy and does not rely on defect specific collective variables. It therefore provides a general route to assign well-defined free energies to individual metastable basins, even when these basins are separated by low barriers. In this setting, BABFc enables stable, bias corrected free energy estimates with statistical accuracies at the meV/atom level and a very low failure rate, including for systems containing approximately one thousand atoms. We demonstrate this capability through thousands of independent free energy calculations covering hundreds of four-interstitial and four-vacancy configurations in bcc {\alpha}-Fe over a broad temperature range, using both a traditional empirical potential and a data driven force field. The study also highlights the critical role of energy landscape regularity in defect thermodynamics. This approach has many powerful applications, ranging from building extensive databases of free energies for data-driven force fields to enabling fully automated workflows for characterizing defects in materials at finite temperatures.
item.dc:creator: Clovis Lapointe, Anruo Zhong, Manuel Ath\`enes, Mihai-Cosmin Marinica

item.title: Discrete-time Kuramoto model with phase lag: Linear stability analysis and onset of synchronization
item.description: arXiv:2609.22715v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate the discrete-time version of the Kuramoto model with phase lag, which comprises globally-coupled phase oscillators of distributed frequencies that are evolving under a nonlinear map. In the continuum limit of an infinite number of oscillators ($N\to \infty$), we derive the exact Frobenius-Perron equation for the time evolution of the single-oscillator probability density, and study linear stability of the incoherent state. Instability signals onset of synchronization. The corresponding synchronization threshold is obtained analytically for the case of a Lorentzian distribution of the oscillator frequencies. The threshold differs from that of the continuous-time Kuramoto model, reflecting the fundamentally different stability conditions for discrete-time maps and continuous-time flows. Beyond synchronization threshold, we observe several interesting nonlinear phenomena: Unlike the classical Kuramoto model, the discrete-time version exhibits periodic and chaotic states. Numerical simulations of the finite-$N$ system confirm the analytical prediction for the synchronization threshold, while highlighting breakdown of the celebrated Ott-Antonsen ansatz invoked to conveniently study the continuous-time Kuramoto model in terms of a low-dimensional description.
item.dc:creator: Prashant M. Gade, Shamik Gupta
